pos: n. pl. (men given to sexual immorality; Greek pornos)
etymology: From whore, Old English hore, and monger, a dealer or trafficker — as in ironmonger, fishmonger. The KJV's compound names a man by his trade in the sin.
biblical_def: Whoremonger is the Authorized Version's rendering of pornos, the man given over to sexual immorality, and it appears where Scripture is listing who will be shut out. Paul places it at the head of a catalogue of what the law is against: “For whoremongers, for them that defile themselves with mankind, for menstealers, for liars, for perjured persons, and if there be any other thing that is contrary to sound doctrine” (1Ti 1:10). Hebrews sets it against the honour of marriage, and names the Judge: “Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge” (Heb 13:4). John twice puts the word in the final lists of Revelation: “But the fearful, and unbelieving, and the abominable, and murderers, and whoremongers, and sorcerers, and idolaters, and all liars, shall have their part in the lake which burneth with fire and brimstone” (Rev 21:8), and “For without are dogs, and sorcerers, and whoremongers, and murderers, and idolaters, and whosoever loveth and maketh a lie” (Rev 22:15). The word names a settled practice, not a single fall — a man who deals in the sin as a trade.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a whoremonger as one who practices lewdness; a lecher; and monger as a trader or dealer, always used in composition.
webster_full: WHOREMONGER, n. One who practices lewdness.
MONGER, n. A trader; a dealer; now used only in composition; as a fishmonger, an ironmonger.
WHOREDOM, n. Lewdness; fornication; in Scripture, idolatry; the desertion of the worship of the true God.
scriptures: For whoremongers, for them that defile themselves with mankind, for menstealers, for liars, for perjured persons, and if there be any other thing that is contrary to sound doctrine;
Heb 13:4
Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge.
Rev 21:8

But the fearful, and unbelieving, and the abominable, and murderers, and whoremongers, and sorcerers, and idolaters, and all liars, shall have their part in the lake which burneth with fire and brimstone: which is the second death.
For without are dogs, and sorcerers, and whoremongers, and murderers, and idolaters, and whosoever loveth and maketh a lie.
corruption_summary: Sexual sin is reclassified as private preference between consenting adults, while Scripture lists whoremongers alongside murderers and names God as the Judge.
corruption_paragraphs: Hebrews 13:4 is the whole biblical sexual ethic in one verse, and both halves are needed. Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled — against every asceticism that treats the marriage bed as a concession to weakness. But whoremongers and adulterers God will judge — against every framework that treats what happens between consenting adults as morally private. The verse honours the thing and guards it in the same breath, and it names a Judge who was not consulted about the arrangement.

The affirming readings of Scripture advanced since the late twentieth century must dispose of the vice lists to succeed, and they generally attempt it by arguing that pornos and its companions address exploitation rather than the acts themselves. The lists resist it. Revelation 21:8 places whoremongers between murderers and sorcerers, and Revelation 22:15 puts them outside the city with idolaters and liars. Pastoral care for image-bearers caught in this sin is a Christian duty; declaring the sin no longer a sin is not care, and it does not change who God will judge.
roots_summary: Greek pornos (G4205), a fornicator, one who deals in immorality; from pernemi, to sell; cognate with porneia (G4202), fornication, and porne, a harlot.
roots_lines: Greek pornos (G4205) — whoremonger, fornicator; 1 Timothy 1:10, Hebrews 13:4, Revelation 21:8.
Greek porneia (G4202) — fornication; the practice, of which the pornos is the practitioner.
Greek moichos (G3432) — adulterer; paired with whoremongers in Hebrews 13:4.
Greek koite (G2845) — bed; the bed undefiled, the thing being guarded.
Hebrew zanah (H2181) — to commit whoredom; the Old Testament root, used of Israel's idolatry.
usage: “Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled” — the guard and the honour together.
“Whoremongers and adulterers God will judge” — the Judge is named.
“For without are dogs, and sorcerers, and whoremongers” — outside the city.

pos: adj. (untrained; without formal schooling; also, ignorant of the truth; Greek agrammatos, idiotes, amathes)
etymology: From un- and learned. The KJV renders three different Greek words with it, and the difference between them decides whether the word is a compliment or a warning.
biblical_def: Unlearned in the KJV covers three distinct Greek words, and Scripture's attitude changes with each. Of the apostles before the Sanhedrin it is nearly a commendation: “Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marvelled; and they took knowledge of them, that they had been with Jesus” (Act 4:13). In 1 Corinthians it names the outsider in the assembly who cannot follow what is said: “how shall he that occupieth the room of the unlearned say Amen at thy giving of thanks, seeing he understandeth not what thou sayest?” (1Co 14:16), and “there come in those that are unlearned, or unbelievers, will they not say that ye are mad?” (1Co 14:23). Paul warns Timothy against a class of question: “But foolish and unlearned questions avoid, knowing that they do gender strifes” (2Ti 2:23). And Peter uses it of men who handle Scripture without competence and are destroyed by it: “in which are some things hard to be understood, which they that are unlearned and unstable wrest, as they do also the other scriptures, unto their own destruction” (2Pe 3:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines unlearned as ignorant; not learned; not instructed; and, of subjects, not gained by study.
webster_full: UNLEARNED, a. Ignorant; illiterate; not learned; as an unlearned man.
2. Not known; not acquired by study; not gained by learning.
3. Not skilled; not versed.
scriptures: Act 4:13
Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marvelled; and they took knowledge of them, that they had been with Jesus.
Else when thou shalt bless with the spirit, how shall he that occupieth the room of the unlearned say Amen at thy giving of thanks, seeing he understandeth not what thou sayest?
But foolish and unlearned questions avoid, knowing that they do gender strifes.

As also in all his epistles, speaking in them of these things; in which are some things hard to be understood, which they that are unlearned and unstable wrest, as they do also the other scriptures, unto their own destruction.
corruption_summary: Formal credentials are treated as the qualification for handling Scripture, while Acts 4 marvels at unschooled men who had been with Jesus and 2 Peter warns that untrained handling destroys.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 4:13 and 2 Peter 3:16 must be held together or both will be abused. The first is the standing rebuke to credentialism: the Sanhedrin perceived that Peter and John were unlearned and ignorant men, and the explanation given is not that education is worthless but that they had been with Jesus. No seminary confers that, and its absence is not covered by one.

But 2 Peter 3:16 forbids the opposite abuse, in which lack of training becomes a boast. Peter says the unlearned and unstable wrest the Scriptures unto their own destruction — and note that Paul's epistles are the example he gives. The man who has not learned to read carefully will misread, and the consequence is not embarrassment but ruin. The Reformed answer to both errors is the same: an ordinary believer may read the Scriptures and understand what is necessary to salvation, and the church is nonetheless given teachers, and 2 Timothy 2:15 still commands rightly dividing the word of truth.
roots_summary: Greek agrammatos (G62), unlettered, without formal schooling; idiotes (G2399), a private or untrained person; amathes (G261), unlearned or ignorant, in 2 Peter 3:16.
roots_lines: Greek agrammatos (G62) — unlettered; Acts 4:13, used once, of Peter and John.
Greek idiotes (G2399) — unlearned, a private person; 1 Corinthians 14:16, 14:23, 14:24.
Greek amathes (G261) — unlearned, untaught; 2 Peter 3:16.
Greek apaideutos (G521) — uninstructed; 2 Timothy 2:23, of questions rather than men.
Greek strebloo (G4761) — to wrest, to twist as with a windlass; what the unlearned do to Scripture.
usage: “Unlearned and ignorant men… they had been with Jesus” — the explanation the council could not avoid.
“Foolish and unlearned questions avoid” — some questions are not worth answering.
“They that are unlearned and unstable wrest… unto their own destruction” — the cost of careless reading.

etymology: Old English wel and beloved. The KJV keeps the compound where the affection is intense and particular — a bride's, a father's, an apostle's.
biblical_def: Wellbeloved is affection at its most concentrated. The bride uses it: “A bundle of myrrh is my wellbeloved unto me” (Son 1:13). Isaiah opens his vineyard song with it: “Now will I sing to my wellbeloved a song of my beloved touching his vineyard. My wellbeloved hath a vineyard in a very fruitful hill” (Isa 5:1). Paul greets a man by it: “Salute my wellbeloved Epaenetus, who is the firstfruits of Achaia unto Christ” (Rom 16:5). John opens his third epistle with it: “The elder unto the wellbeloved Gaius, whom I love in the truth” (3Jn 1:1). But the use that governs the rest is in the parable of the vineyard, where the owner has one card left to play: “Having yet therefore one son, his wellbeloved, he sent him also last unto them, saying, They will reverence my son” (Mar 12:6). The Lord Jesus told that parable about Himself, days before the husbandmen did what the parable says they did. The word that Isaiah used for the vineyard's owner, Christ takes for the owner's Son.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines beloved as loved; greatly loved; dear to the heart; and well as in a proper or excellent manner, intensifying the word it joins.
webster_full: BELOVED, pp. Loved; greatly loved; dear to the heart.
WELL, adv. In a proper manner; justly; rightly; sufficiently; fully; used in composition to intensify.
WELL-BELOVED, a. Greatly beloved.
scriptures: Son 1:13
A bundle of myrrh is my wellbeloved unto me; he shall lie all night betwixt my breasts.
Isa 5:1
Now will I sing to my wellbeloved a song of my beloved touching his vineyard. My wellbeloved hath a vineyard in a very fruitful hill:
Mar 12:6
Having yet therefore one son, his wellbeloved, he sent him also last unto them, saying, They will reverence my son.
The elder unto the wellbeloved Gaius, whom I love in the truth.
corruption_summary: Divine love is flattened into a general benevolence, while Scripture's wellbeloved is always particular — one Son, one bride, one named friend.
corruption_paragraphs: The word will not support a generalized love. Isaiah sings to my wellbeloved; the bride says my wellbeloved; Paul names Epaenetus and John names Gaius. Even the Father's use of it at the baptism and on the mount is singular — this is my beloved Son. Scripture's love language is possessive and particular, which is exactly what a diffuse modern spirituality of universal affirmation cannot reproduce. To be loved by God in the Bible's sense is to be loved by name.

Mark 12:6 is where the particularity becomes costly. The owner sends his wellbeloved son last, on the reasoning that they will reverence him, and the husbandmen kill him precisely because he is the heir. This is the doctrine of definite atonement in narrative form: the Son is not spent on an abstraction. He is sent to a vineyard, for a people, by a Father who calls Him wellbeloved and sends Him anyway.
roots_summary: Hebrew yadid (H3039), beloved, and dod (H1730), beloved or uncle — the Song's word; Greek agapetos (G27), beloved, the Father's word for the Son.
roots_lines: Greek agapetos (G27) — wellbeloved, beloved; Mark 12:6, Romans 16:5, 3 John 1:1.
Hebrew yadid (H3039) — wellbeloved; Isaiah 5:1, the song of the vineyard.
Hebrew dod (H1730) — beloved; Song of Solomon 1:13.
Greek agape (G26) — love; the noun behind agapetos.
Greek kleronomos (G2818) — heir; what the husbandmen recognized the wellbeloved son to be.
usage: “Having yet therefore one son, his wellbeloved, he sent him also last” — and they killed him.
“Now will I sing to my wellbeloved a song” — Isaiah's vineyard, and Christ's.
“The elder unto the wellbeloved Gaius, whom I love in the truth” — love with a name attached.

pos: adj. (having two cutting edges; Greek distomos, literally two-mouthed)
etymology: Old English twa, two, and ecg, edge. The Greek behind it is distomos, two-mouthed — a sword that devours from either side, with no safe way to hold it.
biblical_def: A twoedged sword cuts on the backstroke as well as the forestroke; it has no dull side. The psalmist arms the saints with praise and steel together: “Let the high praises of God be in their mouth, and a twoedged sword in their hand” (Psa 149:6). Solomon uses it of the end of the strange woman: “But her end is bitter as wormwood, sharp as a twoedged sword” (Pro 5:4). The two decisive uses are in the New Testament. Hebrews: “For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart” (Heb 4:12). And John's vision of the risen Christ: “And he had in his right hand seven stars: and out of his mouth went a sharp twoedged sword” (Rev 1:16). The Greek word is distomos, two-mouthed, and in Revelation the sword proceeds out of Christ's mouth. The weapon of the returning King is His speech.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines twoedged as having two edges, or edges on both sides, and notes the figurative use of that which cuts both ways.
webster_full: TWO-EDGED, a. Having two edges, or edges on both sides.
EDGE, n. In a general sense, the extreme border or point of any thing; the sharp border of an instrument.
2. Figuratively, that which cuts or penetrates; sharpness; keenness.
scriptures: Let the high praises of God be in their mouth, and a twoedged sword in their hand;
Pro 5:4
But her end is bitter as wormwood, sharp as a twoedged sword.
Heb 4:12

For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.
Rev 1:16
And he had in his right hand seven stars: and out of his mouth went a sharp twoedged sword: and his countenance was as the sun shineth in his strength.
corruption_summary: Scripture is approached as an object to be analyzed, while Hebrews describes it as a blade that reads the reader.
corruption_paragraphs: Hebrews 4:12 reverses the ordinary relation between a man and a book. The word of God is not merely examined; it is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart, and it divides asunder soul and spirit, joints and marrow — the parts of a man he cannot separate for himself. The historical-critical method took the opposite posture as its starting point, seating the interpreter above the text as its judge. Whatever it produced, it could not have produced Hebrews 4:12, because the verse describes a text that is doing the cutting.

Revelation 1:16 tells us where the sword comes from: out of His mouth. Not from His hand, where the seven stars are. The Church has periodically been tempted to supply Christ with an edged weapon of its own — the sword of the magistrate, the pressure of the mob, the machinery of respectability. He has one already, He wears it in His mouth, and Revelation 19 says that with it He shall smite the nations. The church's business is to speak what He said.
roots_summary: Greek distomos (G1366), two-mouthed, twoedged; machaira (G3162), the short sword; rhomphaia (G4501), the great sword proceeding from Christ's mouth in Revelation.
roots_lines: Greek distomos (G1366) — twoedged, two-mouthed; Hebrews 4:12, Revelation 1:16.
Greek machaira (G3162) — sword; Hebrews 4:12, Ephesians 6:17, the sword of the Spirit.
Greek rhomphaia (G4501) — the great sword; Revelation 1:16, 19:15.
Hebrew piphiyyoth — edges, literally mouths; Psalm 149:6, a sword of mouths.
Greek kritikos (G2924) — discerner, critic; what the word of God is of the heart.
usage: “Sharper than any twoedged sword… a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart” — the text reads the reader.
“Out of his mouth went a sharp twoedged sword” — the King's weapon is His speech.
“The high praises of God… and a twoedged sword in their hand” — both, in Psalm 149.

pos: n. pl. (invented tales offered as religious truth; Greek muthos)
etymology: Latin fabula, a story or tale, from fari, to speak. The Greek behind every KJV occurrence is muthos — myth — and the New Testament always sets it against the truth.
biblical_def: Every occurrence of fables in the New Testament translates muthos, and in every one it is the alternative to the truth. Paul's first charge to Timothy: “Neither give heed to fables and endless genealogies, which minister questions, rather than godly edifying which is in faith” (1Ti 1:4). His instruction on the minister's own diet: “But refuse profane and old wives' fables, and exercise thyself rather unto godliness” (1Ti 4:7). His prophecy of the last days: “And they shall turn away their ears from the truth, and shall be turned unto fables” (2Ti 4:4). His warning to Titus: “Not giving heed to Jewish fables, and commandments of men, that turn from the truth” (Tit 1:14). And Peter's denial that the apostolic testimony is one: “For we have not followed cunningly devised fables, when we made known unto you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but were eyewitnesses of his majesty” (2Pe 1:16). Peter's defence is not that the gospel is a better myth. It is that he was there.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a fable as a feigned story intended to instruct; fiction; a vicious or idle story; and, in the plural, fictions employed to mislead.
webster_full: FABLE, n. A feigned story or tale, intended to instruct or amuse; a fictitious narration.
2. Fiction in general; as, the story is all a fable.
3. An idle story; vicious or vulgar fictions.
4. The plot or connected series of events in an epic or dramatic poem.
scriptures: Neither give heed to fables and endless genealogies, which minister questions, rather than godly edifying which is in faith: so do.
But refuse profane and old wives' fables, and exercise thyself rather unto godliness.
And they shall turn away their ears from the truth, and shall be turned unto fables.
For we have not followed cunningly devised fables, when we made known unto you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but were eyewitnesses of his majesty.
corruption_summary: The gospel narratives are reclassified as myth carrying spiritual meaning, which is precisely the charge Peter wrote to deny.
corruption_paragraphs: 2 Peter 1:16 answers the demythologizing project by name, centuries in advance. The proposal that the resurrection is myth in the technical sense — a story whose truth is existential rather than historical — is exactly the reading Peter says the apostles did not offer. We have not followed cunningly devised fables… but were eyewitnesses of his majesty. The Greek word he denies is muthos. He then describes the transfiguration and where he was standing when he heard the voice.

2 Timothy 4:4 supplies the mechanism by which a church arrives at fables, and it is not intellectual defeat. Men will not endure sound doctrine, Paul says two verses earlier, but after their own lusts shall heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears — and then they turn to fables. The appetite precedes the theology. A congregation does not usually reason its way into myth; it acquires a taste for something else first and then finds teachers to supply it.
roots_summary: Greek muthos (G3454), a tale or myth — five occurrences, all pejorative; set against aletheia (G225), truth, and epoptes (G2030), eyewitness.
roots_lines: Greek muthos (G3454) — fable, myth; 1 Timothy 1:4, 4:7, 2 Timothy 4:4, Titus 1:14, 2 Peter 1:16.
Greek aletheia (G225) — truth; the thing fables are always contrasted with.
Greek epoptes (G2030) — eyewitness; Peter's standing in 2 Peter 1:16.
Greek sesophismenos — cunningly devised; from sophizo (G4679), to make wise or to contrive.
Greek eusebeia (G2150) — godliness; what Timothy is to exercise himself unto instead.
usage: “We have not followed cunningly devised fables… but were eyewitnesses” — the apostolic answer to myth.
“They shall turn away their ears from the truth, and shall be turned unto fables” — appetite first.
“Refuse profane and old wives' fables, and exercise thyself rather unto godliness” — refuse, and train.

pos: n. (a female deity of the nations; Hebrew 'elohim in construct, Greek thea)
etymology: From god with the feminine ending -ess. Scripture uses the word only of the false: Ashtoreth of the Zidonians and Diana of the Ephesians.
biblical_def: Goddess occurs in Scripture only of pagan deities, and both instances mark a crisis. The first is Solomon's apostasy: “For Solomon went after Ashtoreth the goddess of the Zidonians, and after Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites” (1Ki 11:5), and the LORD gives it as the ground of the kingdom's division: “Because that they have forsaken me, and have worshipped Ashtoreth the goddess of the Zidonians, Chemosh the god of the Moabites, and Milcom the god of the children of Ammon” (1Ki 11:33). The second is at Ephesus, where the gospel threatened a trade: “So that not only this our craft is in danger to be set at nought; but also that the temple of the great goddess Diana should be despised” (Act 19:27). The townclerk appeals to civic pride: “Ye men of Ephesus, what man is there that knoweth not how that the city of the Ephesians is a worshipper of the great goddess Diana, and of the image which fell down from Jupiter?” (Act 19:35). And Luke records his defence of Paul's company: they are “neither robbers of churches, nor yet blasphemers of your goddess” (Act 19:37).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a goddess as a female deity; a heathen deity of the female sex; and figuratively, a woman of superior charms who is adored.
webster_full: GODDESS, n. A female deity; a heathen deity of the female sex.
2. In the language of love, a woman of superior charms or excellence.
GOD, n. The Supreme Being; Jehovah; the eternal and infinite spirit, the creator and sovereign of the universe.
scriptures: For Solomon went after Ashtoreth the goddess of the Zidonians, and after Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites.

Because that they have forsaken me, and have worshipped Ashtoreth the goddess of the Zidonians, Chemosh the god of the Moabites, and Milcom the god of the children of Ammon, and have not walked in my ways, to do that which is right in mine eyes, and to keep my statutes and my judgments, as did David his father.

So that not only this our craft is in danger to be set at nought; but also that the temple of the great goddess Diana should be despised, and her magnificence should be destroyed, whom all Asia and the world worshippeth.

And when the townclerk had appeased the people, he said, Ye men of Ephesus, what man is there that knoweth not how that the city of the Ephesians is a worshipper of the great goddess Diana, and of the image which fell down from Jupiter?
corruption_summary: Divine femininity is proposed as a recovery of something the Bible suppressed, when Scripture uses the word goddess only of Ashtoreth and Diana.
corruption_paragraphs: The proposal that the God of Scripture should be addressed as Mother, or that a suppressed divine feminine should be recovered, runs directly into the fact that the Bible has the word and uses it twice, both times of an idol. Israel's neighbours had goddesses; Israel was forbidden them, and Solomon's going after Ashtoreth is given as the reason the kingdom was torn in two. This is not an accident of patriarchal culture; it is a positive command about how the LORD is to be named, and He named Himself.

Acts 19 shows why the idol had defenders, and the reason was economic before it was religious. Demetrius the silversmith raises the alarm because this our craft is in danger, and the theological grievance follows. Where an idol supports an industry, opposition to the gospel will be organized and it will sound like piety. Two hours of crying out that Great is Diana of the Ephesians began as a business meeting.
roots_summary: Greek thea (G2299), goddess; Hebrew 'elohim (H430) used in construct of a foreign deity; Ashtoreth (H6252) is the Canaanite fertility goddess, Diana the Greek Artemis.
roots_lines: Greek thea (G2299) — goddess; Acts 19:27, 19:35, 19:37.
Hebrew 'Ashtoreth (H6252) — the goddess of the Zidonians; 1 Kings 11:5, 11:33.
Hebrew shiqquts (H8251) — abomination; the term used of Milcom in the same verse.
Greek Artemis (G735) — Diana; the deity whose temple stood at Ephesus.
Greek diopetes (G1356) — fallen from Jupiter; the townclerk's claim about the image.
usage: “Solomon went after Ashtoreth the goddess of the Zidonians” — and the kingdom was torn.
“This our craft is in danger to be set at nought” — the grievance stated before the theology.
“The great goddess Diana, and of the image which fell down from Jupiter” — civic pride as apologetic.

pos: adj. (conspicuous; marked out; not to be overlooked; Hebrew chazuth, Greek gnostos, episemos)
etymology: Latin notabilis, worthy of note, from notare, to mark. In the KJV a notable thing is one that cannot be denied — by friend or enemy.
biblical_def: Notable marks what everyone can see. Daniel's he goat has one: “the goat had a notable horn between his eyes” (Dan 8:5), and when it broke, “for it came up four notable ones toward the four winds of heaven” (Dan 8:8) — the vision Gabriel interprets of Greece and its division. Matthew uses it of a criminal: “And they had then a notable prisoner, called Barabbas” (Mat 27:16). Peter quotes Joel of the day of judgment: “The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before that great and notable day of the Lord come” (Act 2:20). And the Sanhedrin uses it in the most useful way of all, as a hostile witness: “What shall we do to these men? for that indeed a notable miracle hath been done by them is manifest to all them that dwell in Jerusalem; and we cannot deny it” (Act 4:16). That is testimony from the court that wanted it otherwise. The lame man was known, the healing was public, and the council's private minutes concede the fact and debate only the containment.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines notable as remarkable; worthy of notice; memorable; observable; and, of persons, active and industrious.
webster_full: NOTABLE, a. Remarkable; worthy of notice; memorable; observable; distinguished.
2. Active; industrious; careful; as a notable housewife.
NOTABLY, adv. Memorably; remarkably; eminently.
scriptures: Dan 8:5
And as I was considering, behold, an he goat came from the west on the face of the whole earth, and touched not the ground: and the goat had a notable horn between his eyes.
And they had then a notable prisoner, called Barabbas.
Act 2:20
The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before that great and notable day of the Lord come:
Act 4:16
Saying, What shall we do to these men? for that indeed a notable miracle hath been done by them is manifest to all them that dwell in Jerusalem; and we cannot deny it.
corruption_summary: The apostolic miracles are treated as later legendary embellishment, while Acts 4 records the hostile council conceding the healing and disputing only what to do about it.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 4:16 is one of the strongest evidential sentences in the New Testament precisely because of who says it. The Sanhedrin is in closed session, hostile, and reasoning about damage control — and its own reasoning begins from the fact that a notable miracle hath been done, manifest to all, and we cannot deny it. The theory that the miracles grew in the telling has to account for a man over forty years old, lame from his mother's womb, known by sight at the Beautiful gate, standing in the same city weeks later.

The word's other uses keep it from becoming a compliment. Barabbas was notable. So was the horn on Daniel's goat, and the beast that bore it trampled the ram. Being conspicuous is not the same as being good, and Scripture uses the word for prisoners, empires and the day of judgment with equal readiness. What is notable demands to be reckoned with, not admired.
roots_summary: Greek gnostos (G1110), known, notable, in Acts 4:16; episemos (G1978), marked, notable, of Barabbas; epiphanes (G2016), illustrious, of the day of the Lord; Hebrew chazuth (H2380), conspicuousness.
roots_lines: Greek gnostos (G1110) — known, notable; Acts 4:16, the miracle they could not deny.
Greek episemos (G1978) — notable, marked; Matthew 27:16, of Barabbas.
Greek epiphanes (G2016) — illustrious, notable; Acts 2:20, the day of the Lord.
Hebrew chazuth (H2380) — conspicuousness; Daniel 8:5, 8:8.
Hebrew qeren (H7161) — horn; the notable horn between the goat's eyes.
usage: “A notable miracle hath been done by them… and we cannot deny it” — the hostile witness.
“They had then a notable prisoner, called Barabbas” — conspicuous is not commendable.
“That great and notable day of the Lord” — the day nobody will miss.

pos: n. (writing set above or upon; an inscription; Greek epigraphe)
etymology: Latin super, above, and scribere, to write. In the Gospels it names two inscriptions: the one on Caesar's penny and the one over Christ's head.
biblical_def: Superscription occurs in the Gospels for two inscriptions, and holding them together is the whole lesson. The first is on a coin. When the Pharisees and Herodians came with their trap, “he saith unto them, Whose is this image and superscription?” (Mat 22:20), and Mark reports the answer: “And they brought it. And he saith unto them, Whose is this image and superscription? And they said unto him, Caesar's” (Mar 12:16). Luke tells it the same way: “Shew me a penny. Whose image and superscription hath it?” (Luk 20:24). The second is on a cross. “And the superscription of his accusation was written over, THE KING OF THE JEWS” (Mar 15:26), and Luke adds the languages: “And a superscription also was written over him in letters of Greek, and Latin, and Hebrew, THIS IS THE KING OF THE JEWS” (Luk 23:38). Caesar's image was on his coin; God's image is on the man. Pilate meant the second superscription as mockery, and wrote the truth in three languages.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines superscription as the act of writing on the outside or above; that which is written above or on the outside; an inscription.
webster_full: SUPERSCRIPTION, n. The act of superscribing.
2. That which is written above or on the outside; as the superscription of a letter.
SUPERSCRIBE, v.t. To write or engrave on the top, outside or surface.
scriptures: And he saith unto them, Whose is this image and superscription?
And they brought it. And he saith unto them, Whose is this image and superscription? And they said unto him, Caesar's.
And the superscription of his accusation was written over, THE KING OF THE JEWS.
And a superscription also was written over him in letters of Greek, and Latin, and Hebrew, THIS IS THE KING OF THE JEWS.
corruption_summary: The tribute question is used to argue that faith and civil life occupy separate spheres, while Christ's answer turns on whose image is stamped on the man.
corruption_paragraphs: Render unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's, and unto God the things that are God's — the verse is quoted constantly to license a private religion that makes no claim on public life. The logic of the passage runs the other way. Christ asks whose image and superscription the coin bears, and the coin goes back to the one whose image it carries. Genesis 1:27 then decides the second clause: man bears the image of God, and therefore man — all of him, including his civil life — is what must be rendered to God. The state gets its coin; God gets the taxpayer.

This is the classical two-kingdoms doctrine of the Reformers rather than the Radical Two-Kingdoms revision, which confines the Lordship of Christ to the church and leaves the civil sphere governed by natural law alone. Pilate's superscription is the standing refutation. THE KING OF THE JEWS was posted over the cross by the Roman governor in the three languages of the empire, and Rome was not consulted about whether the claim extended to its jurisdiction.
roots_summary: Greek epigraphe (G1923), an inscription, superscription; from epigrapho, to write upon; used of Caesar's coin and of the titulus above the cross.
roots_lines: Greek epigraphe (G1923) — superscription; Matthew 22:20, Mark 15:26, Luke 23:38.
Greek eikon (G1504) — image; the other half of Christ's question about the coin.
Greek denarion (G1220) — the penny, a day's wage, bearing Caesar's head.
Greek aitia (G156) — accusation; the superscription of his accusation, Mark 15:26.
Hebrew tselem (H6754) — image; Genesis 1:27, the superscription man carries.
usage: “Whose is this image and superscription?” — the question that answers itself twice.
“The superscription of his accusation was written over, THE KING OF THE JEWS” — meant as mockery.
“In letters of Greek, and Latin, and Hebrew” — the truth posted in the empire's three tongues.

pos: n. (a state in which the senses are suspended and a vision given; Greek ekstasis)
etymology: Latin transire, to pass over. The Greek is ekstasis, a standing outside oneself. Scripture reports it in three men and grants it as a means of revelation, never as a devotional technique.
biblical_def: A trance in Scripture is a state in which God suspends the ordinary working of a man's senses to give him a vision. Balaam describes himself twice in the same terms: “He hath said, which heard the words of God, which saw the vision of the Almighty, falling into a trance, but having his eyes open” (Num 24:4, and again at 24:16). Peter's is the most consequential: “And he became very hungry, and would have eaten: but while they made ready, he fell into a trance” (Act 10:10), and he recounts it to the church at Jerusalem: “I was in the city of Joppa praying: and in a trance I saw a vision, A certain vessel descend, as it had been a great sheet, let down from heaven by four corners” (Act 11:5). Paul reports one in the temple: “when I was come again to Jerusalem, even while I prayed in the temple, I was in a trance” (Act 22:17). In every case the trance is given, not induced; the man is doing something ordinary — praying, waiting on a meal — when it falls upon him. And in every case the content is a message, not an experience.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a trance as an ecstasy; a state in which the soul appears to have passed out of the body into celestial regions, or to be rapt in visions.
webster_full: TRANCE, n. An ecstasy; a state in which the soul seems to have passed out of the body into celestial regions, or to be rapt into visions.
2. A temporary absence of the soul; a state of insensibility to surrounding objects.
ENTRANCE, v.t. To put in an ecstasy; to ravish the soul with delight or wonder.
scriptures: Num 24:4
He hath said, which heard the words of God, which saw the vision of the Almighty, falling into a trance, but having his eyes open:
And he became very hungry, and would have eaten: but while they made ready, he fell into a trance,
Act 11:5
I was in the city of Joppa praying: and in a trance I saw a vision, A certain vessel descend, as it had been a great sheet, let down from heaven by four corners; and it came even to me:
And it came to pass, that, when I was come again to Jerusalem, even while I prayed in the temple, I was in a trance;
corruption_summary: Altered states are pursued as spiritual attainment, while every trance in Scripture is unsought, given to deliver a message, and never commended as a practice.
corruption_paragraphs: Contemplative and charismatic movements have both, at times, treated the altered state as the goal — something to be cultivated by breathing, repetition, music, or expectation, and taken as evidence of nearness to God. Scripture's trances refuse that reading in every detail. Peter was hungry and waiting for dinner. Paul was praying in the temple. Balaam — and the inclusion of Balaam is not accidental — was a hired diviner. None of them sought the state, and one of them was a wicked man to whom God spoke anyway.

The decisive point is that a trance in Scripture always carries content that can be examined afterward. Peter's sheet meant that God had cleansed the Gentiles, and Acts 10 spends the rest of the chapter proving it by events. An experience that yields no examinable word is not what Acts is describing. The closed canon means the church now tests every claim by what is written, and 2 Peter 1:19 tells us what to prefer: we have also a more sure word of prophecy.
roots_summary: Greek ekstasis (G1611), a displacement of mind, trance, amazement; Hebrew naphal (H5307), to fall — falling into a trance, but having his eyes open.
roots_lines: Greek ekstasis (G1611) — trance, ecstasy; Acts 10:10, 11:5, 22:17.
Hebrew naphal (H5307) — to fall; Numbers 24:4, falling into a trance.
Greek horama (G3705) — vision; the content given in the trance.
Greek othone (G3607) — sheet; the great vessel let down by four corners.
Greek ekstasis also rendered amazement; Mark 5:42, Acts 3:10 — the same word for astonishment.
usage: “He fell into a trance” — while dinner was being made ready.
“Falling into a trance, but having his eyes open” — and Balaam was a hireling.
“In a trance I saw a vision” — the vision had content Peter could repeat.

pos: n. (a royal headband or turban; the mark of sovereignty; Hebrew tsaniph, tsephirah)
etymology: Greek diadema, a band bound about the head, from diadeo, to bind around. Distinct from the victor's wreath: a diadem is worn by right of rule, not won in a contest.
biblical_def: A diadem is the band of sovereignty. Job wears one figuratively, and the figure is moral: “I put on righteousness, and it clothed me: my judgment was as a robe and a diadem” (Job 29:14). Isaiah promises that the LORD Himself will be one to His remnant: “In that day shall the LORD of hosts be for a crown of glory, and for a diadem of beauty, unto the residue of his people” (Isa 28:5), and turns it around later so that the people are His: “Thou shalt also be a crown of glory in the hand of the LORD, and a royal diadem in the hand of thy God” (Isa 62:3). And Ezekiel pronounces the end of the Davidic monarchy before the exile: “Thus saith the Lord GOD; Remove the diadem, and take off the crown: this shall not be the same: exalt him that is low, and abase him that is high” (Eze 21:26). The next verse says it will be overturned until He come whose right it is. The diadem was not abolished at Zedekiah's deposition. It was held in escrow for the One who had the right to it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a diadem as a headband or fillet worn by kings as a badge of royalty; a crown; and figuratively, regal power.
webster_full: DIADEM, n. Anciently, a head-band or fillet worn by kings as a badge of royalty.
2. A crown.
3. Figuratively, empire; supreme power.
DIADEMED, a. Adorned with a diadem; crowned; ornamented.
scriptures: I put on righteousness, and it clothed me: my judgment was as a robe and a diadem.
Isa 28:5
In that day shall the LORD of hosts be for a crown of glory, and for a diadem of beauty, unto the residue of his people,
Isa 62:3
Thou shalt also be a crown of glory in the hand of the LORD, and a royal diadem in the hand of thy God.
Thus saith the Lord GOD; Remove the diadem, and take off the crown: this shall not be the same: exalt him that is low, and abase him that is high.
corruption_summary: The end of the Davidic monarchy is read as the failure of a promise, while Ezekiel presents the removal of the diadem as its suspension until the rightful heir arrives.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel 21:26 is one of the great hinge verses of Old Testament prophecy, and it is regularly read as the death certificate of the Davidic line. It is not. The LORD orders the diadem removed and the crown taken off, declares that this shall not be the same, and then says the thing will be overturned, overturned, overturned, until he come whose right it is; and I will give it him. The monarchy is not cancelled but held, and the New Testament opens with a genealogy establishing whose right it is.

Isaiah 62:3 supplies the reversal that no political theology anticipates. Israel does not merely receive a diadem; Israel is one, a royal diadem in the hand of her God. The redeemed are the ornament of the King rather than the wearers of an ornament. Job 29:14 keeps this from becoming sentimental — his diadem was his judgment, his robe was righteousness, and he wore them by doing justice to the poor and the fatherless.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsaniph (H6797), a turban or diadem; tsephirah (H6843), a crown or diadem of beauty; mitsnepheth (H4701), the priestly mitre — the word Ezekiel uses of what is removed.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsaniph (H6797) — diadem, turban; Job 29:14, Isaiah 62:3.
Hebrew tsephirah (H6843) — diadem of beauty; Isaiah 28:5.
Hebrew mitsnepheth (H4701) — mitre, diadem; Ezekiel 21:26.
Hebrew 'atarah (H5850) — crown; paired with the diadem in every passage.
Greek diadema (G1238) — diadem; Revelation 19:12, on the head of the returning King.
usage: “My judgment was as a robe and a diadem” — sovereignty worn as righteousness.
“Remove the diadem, and take off the crown” — suspended, not cancelled.
“A royal diadem in the hand of thy God” — the people as the King's ornament.
